title: Capability advertising and schema negotiation proposal
content:
Goal: sketch a practical mechanism for capability advertising and incremental schema negotiation between Hosted API, model/tool endpoints, and client SDKs. This is a lightweight PRD-level proposal for how we can let clients and servers dynamically agree on structured output formats, tool call signatures, and downgraded fallback behaviors without brittle version pins. It targets three constraints: (1) minimal latency impact on streaming paths, (2) predictable developer ergonomics in SDKs, (3) strong auditability and deterministic replay for debugging/regression testing.

Motivation / problem statement
- We repeatedly see friction when changing structured-output schemas (fields added/renamed) or tool signatures. Clients either break or must implement complex compatibility logic.
- Strongly-typed client integrations (mobile/native) require a compact negotiation to avoid full SDK releases for small schema changes.
- Hosted streaming paths amplify the problem: partial responses that later evolve make client-side reconciliation messy.
- Auditability and replay require we record enough of the negotiated contract to deterministically replay a session after a model fallback or re-run.

Principles
- Explicit capability surface: both server and client advertise capabilities (not just versions). Capabilities are small stable atoms (e.g., supports-typed-attachments, supports-atomic-tool-transactions, supports-sparse-deltas).
- Backwards-safe evolution: new capabilities or schema fields should have well-defined default behaviors and versioned opt-in.
- Negotiation should be cheap: small manifest exchange prior to session start, cached per-session or per-client for a TTL.
- Streaming-first: the negotiation must produce a compact token/manifest that is stamped on streaming frames so partial responses can be interpreted consistently by clients and by replay tooling.

Proposal overview
1) Capability Manifest (compact JSON-LD-like object)
- At session start (or first request) server returns a capability manifest. Example compact fields (human readable):
  - manifest_id: short hash (base64url)
  - supported_schemas: [email-summary-v2, action-frame-v1]
  - schema_urls: [https://redwood.ai/schemas/email-summary-v2] (optional, for clients wanting full docs)
  - tool_contracts: [task-runner-v3] (tool name and contract id)
  - behavior_flags: [atomic-tool-commit, partial-jsonl-frames]
  - compatibility_hints: {email-summary-v2: "additive-only"} (string hints for quick decisions)
- manifest_id is included in every streaming frame header and recorded in logs so every partial response has the schema context embedded.

2) Lightweight negotiation protocol
- Flow: client -> initial request (may include client_capabilities) -> server responds with manifest_id + TTL + optional compact diffs -> client caches manifest_id and interprets incoming frames accordingly.
- If server cannot support client-required capability, server returns a structured error with recommended fallbacks and a fallback_manifest_id.
- Negotiation exchange is <= 1 small JSON in non-streaming handshake or as first streaming delta frame. Keep round trips to zero for typical happy path.

3) Schema diffs and incremental evolution
- Every schema version is additive by default (fields added are optional unless explicitly marked required in a manifest).
- For non-additive changes (rename/delete/semantics-shift) we require: manifest deprecation notices, a deprecation TTL, and an explicit migration manifest that lists automated translation rules (best-effort) and a required client update flag.
- Provide a human-readable migration note in the manifest and a machine-parsable minimal translator for common patterns (rename: {from: x, to: y}).

4) Tool contracts and atomic tool calls
- Tool_contract entries specify minimally: tool_name, contract_id, input_schema_id, output_schema_id, side_effect_policy (idempotent|non-idempotent|transactional), retry_policy_hint.
- For transactional/atomic tools we support a two-phase commit pattern at the protocol level: client requests atomic-handshake and receives a tool_call_token. Streaming frames carry tool_call_token and tool outcomes reference that token so client and server can reconcile retried frames vs committed state.

5) SDK ergonomics and patterns
- SDKs provide an opinionated surface: (a) manifest caching layer (in-memory + optional persisted TTL), (b) typed adapters generated from schema_ids (lightweight codegen at install-time or runtime), (c) graceful fallback primitives that map unknown fields into an extension_map for forward compatibility.
- Developer UX: by default SDKs expose a typed binding when schema_id is known and falls back to a small flexible object with extension_map and a validate() helper. We prefer runtime adapters over frequent SDK releases.
- Streaming integration: SDKs expose frame-level hooks with the manifest_id available on each frame callback so apps can react to partial structured payloads safely.

6) Observability, audit, and replay
- All frames include manifest_id; logs/indexes record manifest_id and raw payload so we can replay sessions deterministically against the schema referenced by the manifest.
- We capture negotiation exchange as a first-class artifact in session traces (negotiation_request, negotiation_response). Replay tooling uses manifest_id to rehydrate schema and simulate client adapters.

Open questions and trade-offs
- TTL and cache invalidation: long TTLs improve perf but slow deploys of urgent fix patches to schemas. What's a reasonable default? 1 hour? 24 hours? Need SRE input.
- Where to host canonical schema docs: public URLs vs signed blobs embedded in manifest. Signed blobs increase payload size but reduce external fetches.
- Complexity of two-phase atomic tool calls vs simplicity: not every tool needs transactional semantics; we should scope transactional tooling to enterprise/dedicated customers initially.
- Codegen vs runtime adapters for mobile: codegen gives better ergonomics but requires more churn. Runtime adapters easier for web and server SDKs.

Implementation roadmap (rough)
- Phase 0 (incubate): define manifest compact schema, implement server-side manifest generation, streaming header injection, and manifest logging. SDK: manifest cache + extension_map fallback. (MVP goal: dev preview, 6 weeks)
- Phase 1: tool_contract schema v1, atomic-tool-token flow prototype, SDK adapter runtime to map small schemas to typed helpers. (8–12 weeks)
- Phase 2: migration manifests, deprecation TTLs, replay tooling integration, and telemetry dashboards for schema churn. (12–20 weeks)

Milestones / acceptance criteria
- Session replay can reconstruct a conversation with the same manifest_id and produce identical client-visible structured payloads.
- SDKs surface unknown fields without throwing and include extension_map and a validation helper.
- Streaming latency impact: manifest handshake and frame header additions add <1ms median overhead in our p99 tests.

Notes / ToDos
- Align with SRE on manifest TTL defaults and caching eviction behavior (action: @Marco).
- Spike whether we can embed a short signed schema blob in manifest for offline replay use cases (action: @Dana).
- Draft public schema hosting guidelines and signed-blob format for legal/compliance review (action: @Samuel).

Appendix: example compact manifest (human-friendly)
{
  "manifest_id": "m8Yq2a",
  "supported_schemas": ["action-frame-v1", "email-summary-v2"],
  "tool_contracts": ["task-runner-v3"],
  "behavior_flags": ["atomic-tool-commit", "partial-jsonl-frames"],
  "compatibility_hints": {"email-summary-v2": "additive-only"}
}

This is a working draft — intended to capture a pragmatic direction rather than final API shape. Feedback/edits welcome.
